blocks.directed: [long pause] Śiva Sūtras 2.2
[slowly] प्रयत्नः साधकः
Prayatnaḥ sādhakaḥ.
Effort is effective in accomplishment.

blocks.text: Stop Trying So Hard, but Also Don’t Stop Trying.
blocks.directed: Stop Trying So Hard, but Also Don’t Stop Trying.
[short pause] Right.
Now we’re discussing effort.
Which is already slightly concerning.

blocks.text: Because every spiritual tradition seems to alternate between two completely contradictory instructions.
blocks.directed: Because every spiritual tradition seems to alternate between two completely contradictory instructions.
[short pause] “Make an enormous effort.”
[short pause] “Stop making an effort.”
[short pause] “Practise constantly.”
[short pause] “There’s nothing to attain.”
[short pause] “Apply yourself.”
[short pause] “Let go.”

blocks.text: And the poor practitioner is sitting in the middle, thinking:
blocks.directed: [short pause] And the poor practitioner is sitting in the middle, thinking:

blocks.text: CAN SOMEBODY PLEASE TELL ME WHAT I’M SUPPOSED TO BE DOING WITH MY EYEBROWS?
blocks.directed: CAN SOMEBODY PLEASE TELL ME WHAT I’M SUPPOSED TO BE DOING WITH MY EYEBROWS?

blocks.text: Fortunately, Vasugupta is talking about a rather specific kind of effort.
blocks.directed: Fortunately, Vasugupta is talking about a rather specific kind of effort.
Prayatna — effort, exertion, endeavour.

blocks.text: Sādhaka — that which accomplishes, or the effective means of attainment. The word also commonly denotes a practitioner, but here Kṣemarāja emphasises the efficacy of the effort.
blocks.directed: Sādhaka — that which accomplishes, or the effective means of attainment. The word also commonly denotes a practitioner, but here Kṣemarāja emphasises the efficacy of the effort.

blocks.text: Now, when Kṣemarāja explains this, he doesn’t simply recommend forcing the mind into submission through sheer muscular determination.
blocks.directed: Now, when Kṣemarāja explains this, he doesn’t simply recommend forcing the mind into submission through sheer muscular determination.

blocks.text: He describes an effort rooted in the spontaneous arising of the desire to contemplate the mantra’s true nature.
blocks.directed: He describes an effort rooted in the spontaneous arising of the desire to contemplate the mantra’s true nature.
This is extraordinarily subtle.

blocks.text: Because we’re dealing with the relationship between icchā, jñāna and kriyā.
blocks.directed: Because we’re dealing with the relationship between icchā, jñāna and kriyā.
Will.
Knowledge.
Action.
Imagine you’re contemplating Śiva.
Perhaps repeating a mantra.

blocks.text: Perhaps reflecting on the nature of awareness.
blocks.directed: Perhaps reflecting on the nature of awareness.

blocks.text: Suddenly there’s a genuine movement towards recognition.
blocks.directed: Suddenly there’s a genuine movement towards recognition.

blocks.text: Not merely the thought, “I should meditate because my schedule says so.”
blocks.directed: Not merely the thought, “I should meditate because my schedule says so.”

blocks.text: But a living impulse towards the source of awareness.
blocks.directed: But a living impulse towards the source of awareness.

blocks.text: An interest so immediate that the mind naturally turns towards it.
blocks.directed: An interest so immediate that the mind naturally turns towards it.

blocks.text: Kṣemarāja says the practitioner must firmly seize this arising.
blocks.directed: Kṣemarāja says the practitioner must firmly seize this arising.

blocks.text: And he illustrates the process with imagery taken from the Tantrasadbhāva.
blocks.directed: And he illustrates the process with imagery taken from the Tantrasadbhāva.

blocks.text: A bird sees food and moves towards it with spontaneous intensity.
blocks.directed: A bird sees food and moves towards it with spontaneous intensity.

blocks.text: An arrow, released from its bow, travels towards its target.
blocks.directed: An arrow, released from its bow, travels towards its target.

blocks.text: The point isn’t to strain continuously.
blocks.directed: The point isn’t to strain continuously.

blocks.text: It’s that a particular, concentrated movement of attention can arise with remarkable naturalness.
blocks.directed: It’s that a particular, concentrated movement of attention can arise with remarkable naturalness.
And the practitioner follows it.

blocks.text: This is the difference between distracted, mechanical effort and living contemplative engagement.
blocks.directed: This is the difference between distracted, mechanical effort and living contemplative engagement.

blocks.text: Consider trying to remember somebody’s name.
blocks.directed: Consider trying to remember somebody’s name.
You sit there.
[short pause] “What’s his name?”
[short pause] “Starts with an M.”
[short pause] “No, perhaps a B.”
You force it.
Nothing.
Then something shifts.
A connection appears.
Suddenly the name becomes obvious.

blocks.text: The breakthrough isn’t merely the product of pushing harder.
blocks.directed: The breakthrough isn’t merely the product of pushing harder.

blocks.text: But neither is it completely unrelated to the preceding attention.
blocks.directed: But neither is it completely unrelated to the preceding attention.

blocks.text: There was a directed engagement, and then an opening.
blocks.directed: There was a directed engagement, and then an opening.

blocks.text: That’s only an analogy, not an equation between memory recall and divine recognition.
blocks.directed: That’s only an analogy, not an equation between memory recall and divine recognition.

blocks.text: But it captures something about the interplay between effort and spontaneous illumination.
blocks.directed: But it captures something about the interplay between effort and spontaneous illumination.

blocks.text: Kṣemarāja is particularly interested in directing the mind towards bindu, here understood as the undivided light of consciousness.
blocks.directed: Kṣemarāja is particularly interested in directing the mind towards bindu, here understood as the undivided light of consciousness.

blocks.text: The effective effort does not consist in collecting more mental objects.
blocks.directed: The effective effort does not consist in collecting more mental objects.

blocks.text: It moves towards the conscious source.
blocks.directed: It moves towards the conscious source.

blocks.text: And the ultimate result is identification with the deity of the mantra.
blocks.directed: And the ultimate result is identification with the deity of the mantra.

blocks.text: The practitioner, the contemplation, and its supreme object cease to be apprehended as fundamentally separate.
blocks.directed: The practitioner, the contemplation, and its supreme object cease to be apprehended as fundamentally separate.
[short pause] So the advice is not:
[short pause] “Just relax, mate, you’re already Śiva.”
[short pause] Nor is it:

blocks.text: “Clench every spiritual muscle until enlightenment pops out.”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “Clench every spiritual muscle until enlightenment pops out.”
[short pause] It’s something closer to:

blocks.text: When the movement towards recognition arises, enter it wholeheartedly.
blocks.directed: When the movement towards recognition arises, enter it wholeheartedly.
Don’t get distracted.

blocks.text: Don’t substitute a theory of recognition for recognition itself.
blocks.directed: Don’t substitute a theory of recognition for recognition itself.

blocks.text: Don’t spend the entire meditation writing an imaginary academic paper about what the meditation would mean if you were actually doing it.
blocks.directed: Don’t spend the entire meditation writing an imaginary academic paper about what the meditation would mean if you were actually doing it.
The Sanskrit is prayatna.
Not procrastinationa.
